AsyncLocalStorage lets you keep per-request data (request id, user, logger) available anywhere in the async call chain without threading it through every function argument. The overhead is small but not zero, and it is rarely the bottleneck compared with I/O; I'd measure it on our own request path before worrying. It would also be a clean way to carry the request id we were just looking at into the logger and the Sentry tag.

Next runs middleware on the edge runtime so it can execute before routing and caching, close to the user, with fast cold starts and low cost. The tradeoff is that you only get Edge-compatible APIs, so no fs and no native Node modules. Newer Next releases added an option to run middleware on the Node.js runtime, but I'd check which Next version we're on before relying on that.

They are not the same. Keep-alive only reuses a TCP connection for requests that go one after another, so a slow response blocks the next one on that connection, which is why browsers open several connections per host. HTTP/2 multiplexes many concurrent request/response streams as interleaved frames over one connection; the remaining weakness is TCP-level head-of-line blocking on packet loss, which HTTP/3 addresses.

`JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x))` only keeps what JSON can represent: Dates become strings, Map and Set become empty objects, undefined and functions disappear, and circular references throw. `structuredClone` keeps Dates, Maps, Sets, typed arrays and handles cycles, but still can't copy functions and drops class prototypes. So the reviewer is probably right if the data holds any of those types.
Action: Look at the flagged usage in the PR to see what data it copies and whether `structuredClone` is a safe swap.
